# themachinethatgoesping nanobind binding style

The **nanobind-specific** conventions. For the underlying C++ class (file layout, naming, comments &
mkdoc docstrings, ObjectPrinter printing, processed-member/unit rules, enums, tests) see
**tmtgp-cpp-class-style**; build/test/install with **tmtgp-build-and-test**. Study `py_kmall` and
`py_s7k` as canonical examples; match the surrounding file.

## Split mode / abi3 (keep bindings limited-API-safe)
Extensions build in **split mode** by default (meson `split_mode`, abi3 frontend + shared
`nanobind_backend`; see **tmtgp-build-and-test**). Practical rule for binding code: **use only the
nanobind API** — it is limited-API (abi3) safe. Do **not** call non-limited CPython C-API
(`PySequence_Fast_GET_SIZE/_ITEMS`, `PyList_GET_ITEM`, `->ob_*`, `->tp_*`, direct numpy C-API, …);
such calls fail to compile under `Py_LIMITED_API`. `nb::ndarray` and the xtensor-python **nanobind**
caster (`<xtensor-python/nanobind/pytensor.hpp>`) are abi3-safe; the pybind11 variant and the numpy
C-API are not. New `.def`s, enums, containers and `bind_vector`s need no split-mode-specific changes.

## Binding file naming
- `c_<class>.cpp` binds exactly **one** class (an `init_c_<class>(module&)`); `module.{hpp,cpp}` per
  submodule (`def_submodule(...)` + calls the per-class `init_c_*`); `init_m_<format>` at the top.
- Namespaces `themachinethatgoesping::echosounders::pymodule::py_<format>[::py_datagrams[::substructs]|
  ::py_filedatacontainers|::py_filedatainterfaces]`.
- Include the C++ headers as `<themachinethatgoesping/echosounders/<fmt>/…>` (angle brackets).

## Module layout (mirror `py_kmall` / `py_s7k`)
Split a format's bindings into submodules, each with its own `module.{hpp,cpp}` that `def_submodule`s
and calls the per-class `init_c_*`:
- `py_<fmt>/` (top) — `def_submodule("<fmt>")`, register the enum `.value(...)` + `make_option_class<o_...>`
  + the free `datagram_type_to_string`/`_from_string`, then call the submodule inits and
  `init_c_<fmt>filehandler` (**stays top-level**).
- `py_<fmt>/py_datagrams/` — **one `c_<datagram>.cpp` per datagram** (+ `substructs/` for per-beam
  substructs & containers, registered into the same `datagrams` submodule). Classes land at
  `<fmt>.datagrams.<Class>`. Register each substruct/container `init_c_*` **before** the datagrams that
  expose them.
- `py_<fmt>/py_filedatacontainers/` — `create_DatagramContainerTypes<...>` for the header, unknown, and
  whole-file variant iterator return types.
- `py_<fmt>/py_filedatainterfaces/` — **split header + cpp**: the interface template
  `<Fmt>DatagramInterface_add_interface_functions<T_BaseClass>(cls)` in a `.hpp`; the
  `py_create_class_<Fmt>DatagramInterface<T_FileStream>` (both stream types) + `init_c_*` in the `.cpp`.

## Both stream types
One template function `py_create_class_<x><T_FileStream>(module&, name)`; register for both stream types
with names `"<Class>"` (`datastreams::MappedFileStream`) and `"<Class>_stream"` (`std::ifstream`).

## Docstrings (DOC macros) & the passthrough repoint
- Bind with `DOC(themachinethatgoesping, echosounders, <fmt>, <Class>, <member>)`; define a per-file
  `#define DOC_<Class>(ARG) DOC(..., <Class>, ARG)` shortcut, and a **variadic**
  `#define DOC_C(CLASS, ...) DOC(..., CLASS, __VA_ARGS__)` when you need a `Content` path.
- **Trivial passthrough `get_x`/`set_x` have an empty generated doc** → point the `.def` at the backing
  *variable's* doc for **both** getter and setter: direct member `_x` → `DOC_<Class>(x)` (mkdoc strips
  the `_`); packed field `_content.x` → `DOC_C(<Class>, Content, x)`. **A getter that processes the
  value (cast/scale/flag/unit) keeps its own `DOC_<Class>(get_x)`** (it has a real `/** @brief */` doc).
- Docstrings are generated by `python make_pybind_doc.py` (walks the tree → `.docstrings/*.doc.hpp`);
  every public method gets an (empty) doc var so `DOC(...)` always resolves. **mkdoc cannot parse a
  `std::vector<xt::xtensor<...>>`-returning getter** → give that `.def` a plain string-literal
  docstring (single `xt::xtensor<..>` returns are fine).

## Enums & OptionFrozen
- `nb::enum_<t_X>(subm, "<Class>_t_X", "desc").value("name", t_X::name, "doc")...` then
  `tools::nanobind_helper::make_option_class<o_X>(subm, "<Class>_o_X")` (needs `enumhelper.hpp`).
  `make_option_class` registers the implicit `str`/`int`/enum→`o_X` constructors; a plain `nb::enum_`
  argument only accepts an int or an enum member, **never a string**.
- A Python method that takes an identifier (e.g. `datagrams(type)`) should take **`o_X` and
  `switch (type.value)`**, so callers pass the enum, the record number, the name or the alt-name string
  interchangeably; pass `type` straight to the C++ `datagrams<T>(id)` (implicit convert).
- **`nb::enum_<t_X>` cannot cast an UNKNOWN value back to Python** — only a *named* enumerator casts
  out; an unnamed value (a real file's proprietary datagram id, e.g. kmall `#CHE`) makes the caster
  raise `ValueError: <n> is not a valid t_X` (only `nb::is_flag` enums allow arbitrary values, which is
  wrong semantics for an id). So **never return the raw identifier enum — nor a `std::map`/`std::vector`
  keyed by it — across the binding when the value can be outside the named set.** Return a **string**
  (via `datagram_identifier_to_string`, unique per type and never-throwing) or the `o_X` wrapper. The
  generic `DatagramContainer` binds `count_datagrams_per_type` / `find_datagram_types` to the C++
  `count_datagrams_per_type_as_string` / `find_datagram_types_as_string` helpers for exactly this
  reason (string keys survive unknown record types; the raw-enum versions crash on them).

## Option-by-string args → helpful "did you mean" errors
- `make_option_class<o_X>` registers `nb::init_implicit<std::string_view>()`. When a Python **str**
  argument is implicitly converted to `o_X` and the name is invalid, nanobind **swallows** the helpful
  `std::invalid_argument("Invalid enum name: '...'. Valid names are: [...]")` thrown by `Option::set`
  and reports only a generic `TypeError: incompatible function arguments` — the caller never sees the
  valid names. (Hit with `ping.bottom.has_feature("two_way_travel_times")` after that feature was
  renamed to `..._legacy`: the opaque TypeError looked like a "broken feature macro" but was just the
  swallowed invalid-name error.)
- Fix: give the method an **explicit `std::string_view` overload** (registered *in addition* to the
  existing `o_X` overload) that calls
  `tools::nanobind_helper::option_from_string_verbose<o_X>(name, "<what>")`. That helper (in
  `tools_nanobind/enumhelper.hpp`) `magic_enum::enum_cast`s the string and, on failure, throws
  `nb::value_error` with a did-you-mean list (substring matches first, else the 3 closest by
  `levenshtein_distance`) **plus** the full valid-name list — the same helper also powers a
  `std::vector<std::string>` overload for `vector<o_X>` methods.
- Overload resolution makes this safe to add without changing behaviour: for a Python **str** the
  `string_view` overload wins in nanobind's no-convert pass; for a bound **`o_X` object** the `o_X`
  overload still wins (the str overload would need a conversion). So add the string overload everywhere
  a str is the ergonomic input (`has_feature` + the `has_any_of/has_all_of_features` vector methods)
  without disturbing enum-object calls. Worked example: `I_PingCommon_add_interface` in
  `pingprocessing`'s `src/nanomodule/py_datatypes/i_pingcommon.hpp` (define a `feature_from_string`
  lambda once, reuse it in all three overloads).
- Two complementary error layers for `has_feature`: (1) an **invalid name** (not a `t_pingfeature`
  enumerator) → the binding-level did-you-mean `ValueError` above; (2) a **valid name that this ping
  class does not register** (e.g. `bottom.has_feature("av")`, a watercolumn feature) → a *library*-side
  `std::runtime_error` from `I_PingCommon::has_feature(o_pingfeature)` that names the class and lists
  the features actually registered for it (do **not** phrase it as an internal "please report" bug — it
  is a usage error).

## Reusable helpers & trailing macros
- Filehandler: `py_filetemplates::py_i_inputfilehandler::add_default_constructors /
  add_open_file_interface / add_default_containers` (the last adds the `datagram_interface` property).
- Interface: `py_i_datagraminterface::add_InterfaceFunctions`; containers:
  `py_datagramcontainer::create_DatagramContainerTypes`.
- Substruct vectors: `NB_MAKE_OPAQUE(std::vector<Row>)` + bind `get_/set_` + end with
  `nb::bind_vector<std::vector<Row>>(m, "<Row>s_vector")`; container: `def_prop_rw` for the raw vector
  (`nb::rv_policy::reference_internal`) + one `.def` per `get_<field>_tensor` (needs
  `<xtensor-python/nanobind/pytensor.hpp>`; variant returns need `<nanobind/stl/variant.h>`).
  ⚠️ `bind_vector` emits `std::find/count/remove`; on clang-cl/MSVC these fail to compile for a
  packed, all-integer `Row` whose `sizeof` ∉ {1,2,4,8}. Fix it on the C++ `Row` (user-provided
  `operator==`), NOT here — see the Windows SIMD rule in tmtgp-echosounders-lessons-learned.
- End every class with `__PYCLASS_DEFAULT_COPY__/BINARY/PRINTING__(Class)` as applicable.
- **When you add a processed getter to the C++ class, add its `.def` here too** (and re-run
  make_pybind_doc so `DOC(...,get_x_in_<unit>)` resolves).

## Debugging import/bind-time failures (`bad cast`, abort, "type already registered")
A `from themachinethatgoesping.<fmt>_nanopy import *` that dies with **`ImportError: bad cast`**, a
**`Fatal Python error: Aborted`**, or a flurry of **`nanobind: type '<X>' was already registered!`** /
apparent "module re-exec" warnings is almost always a **missing nanobind STL caster header in a
binding TU** — a real C++ bug, *not* nanobind doing something weird. The usual root cause:
- A `.def(...)` casts a value **eagerly at bind time** (module init). This happens for every
  **default argument** `nb::arg("x") = <value>` and for any init-time `m.attr(...) = <value>` /
  `cls.attr(...) = <value>`. nanobind converts that C++ value to Python *right there*, so if the
  caster is missing the failure happens **during import**, not on first call.
- If the file does **not** `#include` the matching `<nanobind/stl/<type>.h>`, that TU instantiates the
  **generic** `type_caster<T>` while sibling TUs (which do include it) instantiate the **specialized**
  one → an **ODR violation**. gcc/Linux usually folds to the working specialized caster (imports fine,
  so you **cannot reproduce it locally**); clang-cl/Windows may fold to the generic one, whose runtime
  cast throws `std::bad_cast` → **Windows-only failure**.

**Why it looks cryptic (error masking):** nanobind's `NB_MODULE` exec wrapper catches the C++
exception and rethrows it as `PyErr_SetString(ImportError, e.what())` — so `std::bad_cast` becomes the
bare string **`bad cast`** with no file/type. The meta `__init__.py` then wraps the import in
`try/except pass` (swallows it), and CPython's **import-retry** re-runs the half-finished module body,
producing the misleading "already registered" / "re-exec" warnings. So those warnings are a *symptom*
of the first init dying partway, not the cause.

**How to localize it fast:** the **last** `type '<X>' was already registered!` line is the last binding
that registered *before* the crash — the failing `.def` is right after it (same or next `init_c_*`).
Inspect that binding's default args / init-time casts and check the file's includes. A module-level
`try/catch` around each `init_m_*`/`init_c_*` that prints `e.what()` + which init ran will pin it on CI
when inspection isn't enough.

**The rule (prevention):** **every binding TU that names an STL type in a `.def` signature or a
default-argument value must `#include` the matching caster header in *that file*** — never rely on a
transitive or unity-build include. Common ones: `<nanobind/stl/optional.h>` (`std::optional`,
`std::nullopt` — e.g. `nb::arg("target_id") = std::nullopt`), `vector.h` (`std::vector<...>{}`),
`map.h`/`unordered_map.h`, `pair.h`, `tuple.h`, `variant.h` (variant returns), `shared_ptr.h`,
`string.h`/`string_view.h`. Reference fix: adding `<nanobind/stl/optional.h>` to `pingprocessing`'s
`src/nanomodule/py_datatypes/i_ping.hpp` for `get_geolocation(..., = std::nullopt)` (it was the only
`std::optional` binding missing the header → Windows `bad cast` at `I_Ping` init). To audit, grep for
`std::<type>` / `= std::nullopt` in `src/nanomodule` and confirm each such file includes its caster.

## `boost::flyweight` across module boundaries → **MUST** be `intermodule_holder` (never shared_ptr / value)
`boost::flyweight<T>` is used deliberately throughout theping (sensor configuration, navigation
interpolator, calibrations, RuntimeParameters, sample vectors, …). It gives **two** things at once:
value **deduplication** *and* an **already-computed hash** carried in the handle. **Never "simplify"
a flyweight to `std::shared_ptr<T>` or to a plain `T`, and never remove it** — doing so throws away
the dedup *and* forces a re-hash. Changing it is only acceptable with a very good reason, a full
performance analysis, and a better alternative.

**Pass a flyweight *as a flyweight* end-to-end — never value→flyweight at a boundary.** Interning
`flyweight<T>(value)` hashes `T`; for a big `T` (e.g. `NavigationInterpolatorLatLon`, which holds a
whole file's navigation) that is expensive and, if done per ping, catastrophic. So the interface
that owns the dedup (`I_NavigationDataInterface::_navigation_interpolators`), the setter
(`PingInfo::set_navigation_interpolator_latlon`), and the member must all use the **same** flyweight
type so the hand-off is a cheap handle copy (the hash is computed exactly once, when the object is
first interned).

**The holder is part of the flyweight *type*, and cross-module flyweights MUST use
`boost::flyweights::intermodule_holder`.** A default (`static_holder`) flyweight factory is a
hidden-visibility Meyers singleton → **one factory per `.so`**. theping's extension modules
(`echosounders_nanopy`, `pingprocessing_nanopy`, …) are independent `.so`s that both link the same
static libs, so a flyweight **interned in one module and ref-count-erased in another** operates on
the *wrong* factory and corrupts the heap → **`MemoryError: bad_array_new_length`** (a `new T[n]`
with garbage `n` inside the factory's hashed container). This is **platform-specific**:
- **Linux/ELF**: the GNU loader gives the singleton a **`STB_GNU_UNIQUE`** symbol → one factory
  process-wide anyway → the bug is **latent** (you *cannot* reproduce it locally, even under
  mimalloc/jemalloc).
- **macOS (Mach-O two-level namespace) / Windows (PE)**: no equivalent → one factory per module →
  **crash**. Surfaces as a macOS/Windows-only CI failure (e.g. `KMALLFileHandler(..., cache=True)`).

`intermodule_holder` forces a **single process-wide factory** shared by all modules, keeping the
dedup *and* refcounted cleanup (no leak) while fixing the crash. It pulls in
`boost::interprocess::ipcdetail::intermodule_singleton`; it compiles and runs on all three platforms
here (proven green on macOS CI — do **not** assume otherwise from a misleading commit message).

**Consistency rule (this is what bites):** because the holder is part of the type, `flyweight<T>` and
`flyweight<T, intermodule_holder>` are **different types**. If you make only *some* of the chain
`intermodule_holder` (e.g. only the PingInfo members, leaving the setters/interface on the default
holder), assignment goes through a **cross-policy conversion that silently re-interns (re-hashes)** —
it may even still compile — so you get the performance hit back *and* a confusing partial fix. Change
the **whole** chain. Define one alias and use it everywhere:
```cpp
// pinginfo.hpp (pingprocessing::datatypes)
using NavigationInterpolatorLatLonFlyweight =
    boost::flyweights::flyweight<navigation::NavigationInterpolatorLatLon,
                                 boost::flyweights::intermodule_holder>;
```
then use that exact type in: the owning interface map + its accessors
(`I_NavigationDataInterface`), the `PingInfo` member, `PingInfo`/`I_Ping` setters, every
`read_pings()` call site (kmall/kongsbergall/simradraw/s7k `*pingdatainterfaceperfile.hpp`), and the
nanobind `set_data` lambda in `c_pinginfo.cpp`. Worked examples: the `*Flyweight` aliases in
`pinginfo.hpp`, and the pre-existing `flyweight<BeamSampleSelection, intermodule_holder>` in
`i_pingwatercolumn.hpp` (same rationale, written out inline). To audit, grep for
`flyweight<navigation::` and confirm **none** are default-holder outside the alias definition.

## No C++ multiple inheritance → "add-interface" helper for a second base
nanobind binds **exactly one** C++ base (`nb::class_<Derived, Base>`); binding two C++ bases is
**unsupported** (nanobind 3.x porting docs). When a class multiply-inherits in C++ (e.g.
`I_PingBottom : public I_PingCommon, public raytracers2::I_MBESRawDetectionInfos`), register it with
the **primary** base only (`nb::class_<I_PingBottom, I_PingCommon>`, and keep that base **first** in
the C++ base list so the pointer offset is 0) and expose the *second* base's methods with a reusable
**`add_interface<T_BaseClass>(cls)`** template helper (same pattern as `I_PingBottom_add_interface`).
- Also register the second base as its **own** standalone `nb::class_<I_MBESRawDetectionInfos>` (no
  base) so functions can **return a reference** to it: `cls.def("get_mbesrawdetectioninfos",
  &T::get_mbesrawdetectioninfos, nb::rv_policy::reference_internal, …)` — a zero-copy down-cast whose
  virtual getters still dispatch to the concrete ping. Concrete owning subclasses that have a *single*
  base (e.g. `MBESRawDetectionData : I_MBESRawDetectionInfos`) bind normally with that base and
  **inherit** the interface `.def`s (only add their `set_`/macros).
- **Cross-subproject DOC + helper duplication:** the helper lives in the nanomodule, and a subproject
  cannot include another subproject's *nanomodule* header, so the add-interface helper
  is **duplicated** once per nanomodule (algorithms `py_i_mbesrawdetectioninfos.hpp` +
  pingprocessing `src/nanomodule/py_datatypes/i_mbesrawdetectioninfos.hpp`). Both reference the **same**
  `DOC(themachinethatgoesping, algorithms, …, I_MBESRawDetectionInfos, …)` macros (the docstrings come
  from the *library* header, reachable via `algorithms_dep`), so the docstrings transition to the ping
  classes automatically — re-document nothing in the child.
- **Overload DOC suffixes:** a no-arg + `BeamSelection&` overload pair → mkdoc names them `name` and
  `name_2`; bind both with `nb::overload_cast<>` / `nb::overload_cast<const pingtools::BeamSelection&>`.

## mkdoc doc-var redefinition from a forward-declared return type
If header A forward-declares `class B;` and returns `B` by value, mkdoc emits a **stub**
`mkd_doc_…_B` into **A's** `.doc.hpp`; when a TU includes both A's and B's doc files you get
`redefinition of 'mkd_doc_…_B'`. Fix: add `// IGNORE_DOC:mkd_doc_…_B` immediately above the forward
declaration and re-run mkdoc (worked example: `MBESRawDetectionData` forward-declared in
`i_mbesrawdetectioninfos.hpp`).

## mkdoc cannot parse a `std::vector<xt::xtensor<...>>` return
`pybind11_mkdoc` (libclang) **aborts the whole class parse** on a getter that returns
`std::vector<xt::xtensor<...>>`, so `DOC()` vars go missing for that getter **and every method
declared after it** (not just itself). Use a plain string-literal docstring for such getters and keep
them **last** in the class. (xtensor getters also need their casters in *that* TU:
`#include <xtensor-python/nanobind/pytensor.hpp>` for an `xt::xtensor` return and
`#include <nanobind/stl/vector.h>` for a `std::vector<...>` of them.) Worked examples: the per-beam /
per-sample tensor getters on the echosounder record containers (see tmtgp-echosounders-lessons-learned
§3).
